title: The Lake That Fell From the Sky

pages.text: Edem and Afrakoma stood on the rim of Lake Bosumtwi in the Ashanti Region, looking down at a lake that was almost perfectly round. ‘Nature does not usually draw circles,’ said Afrakoma. ‘Most lakes look like potatoes.’ Many Ashanti people regard the lake as sacred, so their guide asked them to speak softly and show respect.
sentences: Edem and Afrakoma stood on the rim of Lake Bosumtwi in the Ashanti Region, looking down at a lake that was almost perfectly round.
‘Nature does not usually draw circles,’ said Afrakoma.
‘Most lakes look like potatoes.’ Many Ashanti people regard the lake as sacred, so their guide asked them to speak softly and show respect.
pages.alt: Two students stand on the rim of a round lake in green hills with a guide.

pages.text: Mr Danso asked just one question: ‘If you wanted to explain a round lake, what ideas could you test?’ They wrote three: an old volcano, a very large sinkhole, or something striking the ground from space.
sentences: Mr Danso asked just one question: ‘If you wanted to explain a round lake, what ideas could you test?’ They wrote three: an old volcano, a very large sinkhole, or something striking the ground from space.
pages.alt: The students write three ideas in a notebook with a teacher listening.

pages.text: They checked each idea against the clues. A volcano would leave lava and ash, but geologists did not find them. A sinkhole more than ten kilometres wide would be unlike any ordinary sinkhole. That left an impact.
sentences: They checked each idea against the clues.
A volcano would leave lava and ash, but geologists did not find them.
A sinkhole more than ten kilometres wide would be unlike any ordinary sinkhole.
That left an impact.
pages.alt: Two students tick and cross ideas on a list with the lake behind them.

pages.text: Scientists first suggested an impact in 1931. Later studies found rocks changed by sudden extreme pressure and heat, and tiny pieces of space rock mixed into the crater rocks. ‘That is evidence,’ said Edem. ‘A crater is a bowl-shaped hole made when something hits the ground.’
sentences: Scientists first suggested an impact in 1931.
Later studies found rocks changed by sudden extreme pressure and heat, and tiny pieces of space rock mixed into the crater rocks.
‘That is evidence,’ said Edem.
‘A crater is a bowl-shaped hole made when something hits the ground.’
pages.alt: A diagram of a space rock hitting the ground and making a bowl-shaped crater.

pages.text: Mr Danso added a surprise: glass beads called tektites, found in Côte d’Ivoire, match the lake’s age and chemistry. They are melted rock thrown out by the impact. Tiny ones have even been found in mud from the seabed off West Africa. ‘So the impact scattered material across the region!’ said Afrakoma.
sentences: Mr Danso added a surprise: glass beads called tektites, found in Côte d’Ivoire, match the lake’s age and chemistry.
They are melted rock thrown out by the impact.
Tiny ones have even been found in mud from the seabed off West Africa.
‘So the impact scattered material across the region!’ said Afrakoma.
pages.alt: A map of West Africa with small glass beads marked in Côte d’Ivoire and offshore.

pages.text: How old is the crater? About 1.07 million years. Edem did the sums. ‘Homo sapiens are about 300,000 years old, so the crater is 770,000 years older than our species. And the dinosaurs were long gone.’
sentences: How old is the crater?
About 1.07 million years.
Edem did the sums.
‘Homo sapiens are about 300,000 years old, so the crater is 770,000 years older than our species.
And the dinosaurs were long gone.’
pages.alt: Edem writes dates on a timeline with a lake sketch.

pages.text: They checked the size: the crater rim is about 10.5 km across, and the lake about 8.5 km. Afrakoma worked out the lake’s area if it were a perfect circle: radius 4.25 km, so 3.14 × 4.25 × 4.25 is about 56.7 square kilometres. ‘A hole dug in minutes,’ she said, ‘that has held water for a very long time.’

Afrakoma worked out the lake’s area if it were a perfect circle: radius 4.25 km, so 3.14 × 4.25 × 4.25 is about 56.7 square kilometres.
‘A hole dug in minutes,’ she said, ‘that has held water for a very long time.’
pages.alt: Afrakoma calculates on a notebook page beside a drawing of a circle.

pages.text: On the way home Edem drew three columns: What we know, What we think, What we are still asking. Under still asking he wrote: What was life like in this forest before the impact? What can the mud at the bottom of the lake still tell us? The best way to respect the lake, they agreed, was to keep asking questions and leave it as they found it. The end.

pages.alt: A notebook with three columns held by Edem as the sun sets over the lake.

activities.question: Why did the children set aside the volcano idea?
options: Geologists did not find lava or ash to match it

activities.prompt: If a space rock really hit here, what kinds of clues might scientists look for in the rocks?
options: Rocks changed by sudden heat and pressure

activities.question: How do tektites in Côte d’Ivoire link back to the lake?
options: Their age and chemistry match the Bosumtwi impact

activities.definition: A bowl-shaped hole in the ground, often made by something hitting it.

activities.question: About how much older is the crater than our species (1.07 million years versus about 300,000 years)?

activities.prompt: Put the children’s reasoning in order.
items: Notice that the lake is almost perfectly round.
Check each idea against the evidence.
Write what is known and what is still unknown.

activities.prompt: The guide asked the children to show respect at a sacred place. How do you show respect when you explore places that matter to others?

glossary.definition: Holy or deeply important to a community.
Facts or clues that help show what is true.
A bowl-shaped hole in the ground, often made by something hitting it.
Small pieces of natural glass made when an impact melts rock and throws it out.
